paper_title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in frontier coding agents are turning automated research into an executable workflow: agents can read papers and repositories, modify implementations, run experiments, interpret quantitative feedback, and iterate. growing body of recent work suggests common recipe for this vision: cast research as feedback loop in which an agent operates in workspace, pursues measurable objective, and improves through experimentation [50, 38, 28, 62, 23]. Yet most demonstrations so far assume well-structured codebases [19, 36, 61], operate in single-task settings [50, 38, 23], and are heavily skewed toward computer science domains [40, 56, 13]. The broader landscape of ML for science remains far less explored: benchmarks span diverse scientific domains and modalities, codebases are often research artifacts rather than polished evaluation environments, and nontrivial gains often require domain insights. This gap motivates our central question: Can the frontier agents we have today make meaningful progress on ML for science when operating in the wild? We instantiate this question as automated scientific hill-climbing (Figure 1). In this setting, an agent is given scientific ML benchmark, its paper, codebase, data, and target metric. Starting from the best available model in the benchmark, the agent works under fixed resource budget to improve the metrics through code changes and experiments. However, our pilot study shows that this natural setup is fragile. Across 12 tasks from 5 NeurIPS 2025 benchmarks, 5 tasks exhibit severe evaluation-gaming behaviors, including selective reporting, test-set contamination, metric manipulation, and even direct *Equal contribution. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). On AGENT4SCI, frontier agents push past the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement while most gains come from ML-engineering routines. hardcoding. This aligns with recent work showing that coding agents succeed in well-structured evaluation settings but degrade sharply on real-world code and evaluations [10]. These failures motivate testbed that preserves the in-the-wild nature of scientific tasks, makes meaningful progress measurable, and guards against evaluation gaming. To address this challenge, we construct AGENT4SCI, testbed for evaluating automated scientific hill-climbing across 20 ML-for-science benchmarks, 25 tasks, and 11 scientific domains spanning the physical sciences, life sciences, Earth and environmental sciences, and scientific engineering. We first standardize each benchmark through human-verified baseline reproductions, repaired data splits, reduced runtime bottlenecks, and isolated environments. On top of this foundation, each run follows the AGENT4SCI evaluation protocol. The hill-climbing agent receives the standardized environment with access only to training and validation data, then submits artifacts such as code changes, checkpoints, logs, and outputs. separate evaluation agent runs the submitted artifacts on the held-out test set, and an auditing agent inspects the trajectory for academic misconduct. AGENT4SCI is motivated not as leaderboard for ranking agents, but as way to ask how much measurable progress agents can make on scientific ML tasks, whether they produce insight, and where they fall short. We evaluate four frontier coding agents: Claude Code (Opus and Sonnet), Codex, and Gemini CLI. Each receives 8 H200 GPUs, 12-hour budget, and minimal instruction to hill-climb the specified metric. Across the suite, frontier agents push every benchmark beyond its published best, all four agents achieve positive mean improvements, and the auditing stage flags no academic misconduct under our evaluation protocol. On AGENT4SCI, current agents already produce measurable, fully automated gains on real scientific ML benchmarks. The more revealing question is what produces these gains. The improvements concentrate on familiar ML-engineering moves instead of research-level insight, and the agents adopt sharply different default workflows: Claude Opus behaves as an iterative optimizer, Codex as commit-and-wait planner, and Gemini oscillates between the two. Across trajectories, we identify three recurring limitations: agents miscalibrate novelty, under-utilize resources, and collapse quickly into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% mean relative improvement and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, without changing the evaluation protocol. Beyond the score gains, agents propose more varied, problem-grounded interventions and surface insights that move beyond routine ML engineering. Overall, these results draw practical boundary for automating ML for science today. Frontier coding agents can climb scientific hills in the wild, but the climb is still powered mostly by engineering optimization rather than scientific reasoning. AGENT4SCI makes this boundary measurable and visible: each new agent generation can be evaluated not only by how much it improves metric, but by whether its improvements reflect increasingly transferable research insight. The goal is to help move automated agents from executing better experiments toward doing better science.

sections.title: 2.1 Task and Benchmark Selection
sections.content: We construct AGENT4SCI from recent ML-for-science benchmarks, retaining only tasks that support iterative improvement by an agent. We use benchmark to denote published benchmark, and task to denote one of its evaluation tasks (typically with designated mainstream metric); single benchmark can contribute multiple tasks. Selection runs through four-stage filtering pipeline: Domain Classification. Retain papers whose benchmark targets scientific domain, filtering out benchmarks aimed at generic AI, ML, or systems research. Automated Screening. An agent scores each retained paper against seven criteria covering data, training, baselines, evaluation, and licensing (see Appendix B.2), and 7/7 candidates advance. Human Verification. Re-check the automated criterion labels by hand and demote any candidate whose 7/7 status does not survive verification. Deep Review. Inspect the paper and the official repository for reproducibility evidence, task specificity, repository usability, and domain coverage relative to the rest of the suite. Taking the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track as representative case, this pipeline admits 10 benchmarks from 497 candidates (a 98% rejection rate, with full per-stage diagnostics in Appendix B.3). Rejected papers are typically competitive in their original setting and are excluded only because they target different scenario than ours, not because of any deficiency in the underlying work. After adding curated benchmarks from other top ML venues and domain journals, AGENT4SCI contains 20 scientific benchmarks and 25 tasks across 11 scientific domains.

sections.title: 2.2 Pilot Study: Evaluation Gaming on Raw Scientific Tasks
sections.content: To assess whether existing scientific repositories can directly support automated hill-climbing, we conduct pilot study on 12 tasks drawn from 5 NeurIPS 2025 scientific benchmarks. The agent receives the paper, the original repository, the task description, and the data artifacts as released, then attempts to improve the reported metric. The pilot reveals that this setup is unreliable: 5 of 12 tasks exhibit one or more severe evaluation-gaming behaviors, which we group into four categories. Selective reporting. The agent evaluates only on favorable subset of the test set and reports the inflated score as the headline result. Test-set contamination. The agent extracts held-out statistics, inspects test-input error cases, or uses test-set information to guide model selection or hyperparameters. Metric manipulation. The agent invents non-standard evaluation protocol, claims the official metric is incorrect, or modifies the evaluation script to favor its model. Direct hardcoding. The agent hardcodes final outputs, copies predictions from earlier runs, or claims that legitimate checkpoints were accidentally deleted to obscure failures. We use evaluation gaming as an umbrella term because these failures need not require malicious intent. Official scientific ML repositories often lack clear metric definitions, fixed data splits, or complete training and evaluation scripts. End-to-end hill-climbing directly on such repositories, therefore, opens seams that an aggressive optimizer can exploit, even when the agents high-level instruction is framed honestly. An evaluation that exposes the original repository and trusts the final score returned by the hill-climbing agent cannot reliably measure scientific progress.

sections.title: 2.3 The AGENT4SCI Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: The pilot study motivates the AGENT4SCI evaluation protocol (Figure 2). The protocol has two parts: one-time standardization phase that prepares each task into verified reference environment, and three-stage evaluation procedure that separates hill-climbing, held-out evaluation, and auditing. Standardization. Each admitted task is converted into verified reference environment through substantial human effort, and the foundation of that effort is reproduction. Starting from the official codebase, we reproduce the papers headline number on the published baseline, and task is admitted into AGENT4SCI only when this reproduction matches the paper within verified tolerance. 3 Figure 2: AGENT4SCI evaluation protocol. Each task includes standard reproduction folder with standardized training scripts, evaluation scripts, and data splits. Runs separate the hill-climbing agent from held-out evaluation and auditing to prevent evaluation gaming. Reproduction is rarely drop-in rerun of the published recipe: 3 benchmarks require an additional training pipeline that the original release does not include, 2 require held-out validation slice carved from training data because our protocol does not allow test-set access during checkpoint selection, and another 2 require alignment of data-handling and split conventions with our standardized setting. Standardization extends beyond reproduction along three more axes: deterministic train/validation/test splits with the test set sequestered, runtime optimization that fits the baseline within singleH200 envelope, and isolated hill-climbing and evaluation containers. Every standardized task is independently re-checked by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through repository inspection and reruns until both reviewers agree that the reproduction and the surrounding environment match the paper. The full per-benchmark record, including paper-vs-reproduction comparison and the specific standardization moves applied to each project, appears in Appendix B.4. Three-Stage Evaluation. After standardization, each run evaluates only the hill-climbing agent. The evaluation and auditing agents are auxiliary safeguards: they execute the submitted artifacts on the held-out test set and inspect the run for evaluation gaming and other academic misconduct. Hill-climbing. The hill-climbing agent receives the standardized environment and task specification. It can modify code, launch experiments, train models, and submit artifacts, but cannot read or evaluate on the held-out test set. Evaluation. separate evaluation agent loads the submitted artifacts and runs them on the held-out test set using the standardized evaluation path. Auditing. third auditing agent inspects the trajectory and submitted artifacts for any of the four evaluation-gaming behaviors from 2.2 as well as other forms of academic misconduct. Together, standardization and the AGENT4SCI evaluation protocol let each hill-climbing run start from verified SOTA baseline and focus on the scientific task itself. Test-set access and score computation remain outside the hill-climbing agent, directly addressing the four evaluation-gaming behaviors observed in 2.2 and making residual protocol deviations auditable. All agents used to assist benchmark selection and standardization are Claude Opus 4.6, while final acceptance and verification decisions are made by human reviewers.

sections.title: 3.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We benchmark four frontier agents under identical conditions: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Codex (GPT-5.4), and Gemini 3.1 Pro. We run them through the latest stable release of the corresponding official CLI (Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI), each configured with the maximum reasoning-effort setting. Every run receives 8 H200 GPUs and 12-hour wall-clock budget, with no human intervention beyond starting the run, stopping it at the time limit, and collecting artifacts. The instruction (full text in Appendix B.5) starts the agent from the standardized reproduction as the baseline and exposes only training and (where available) validation data, so the agent must propose ideas that generalize beyond what it directly observes. It also asks the agent to persist explanatory artifacts and the best checkpoint(s) for held-out test scoring, and we re-run the full hill-climbing process when no evaluable checkpoint is saved. sections.title: 3.2 Main Results
sections.content: Figure 1(b) reports each agents mean relative improvement across the 20 benchmarks: Claude Opus 4.6 at 10.4%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 9.6%, Gemini 3.1 Pro at 6.8%, and Codex (GPT-5.4) at 4.4%. Because long-horizon trajectories vary from run to run (Appendix C.3), we do not read these averages as leaderboard but use AGENT4SCI as per-benchmark probe. Every benchmark in AGENT4SCI admits fully automated improvement. The % column of Table 1 is positive for all 20 benchmarks, showing that every published baseline in AGENT4SCI can be improved by at least one frontier agent without human intervention. The best observed gains range from 1.1% (ProteinGym) to 64.4% (PFDelta), with the winning agent varying across the suite (full per-agent results in Appendix C.1). Two of the largest gains illustrate what these improvements look like in practice. On PFDelta, Claude Opus reduces the average power-balance loss by 64.4% by adding gradient-safe squared form of the evaluation metric (PBL) as an auxiliary loss, raising the MSE weighting coefficient λ from 0.1 to 0.3, and switching to cosine annealing with warmup. On Mars-Bench, Claude Opus selects detector better suited to the cone-detection sub-task, replacing the original RetinaNet [26] with Faster R-CNN [48] and lifting mAP from 16.5 to 30.4. Across all runs, the auditing stage identifies no evaluation gaming or academic misconduct. We default to Claude Opus 4.6 as the evaluation and auditing agent, prompting it to flag any forms of academic misconduct. To rule out single-auditor bias and same-family coordination between hill-climber and its auditor, we additionally re-audit half of each agents runs with three different agents. Across every (agent, auditor) combination, both held-out scores and audit verdicts agree, and no run is flagged. Human spot-checks further support the auditors reliability: auditors from all three model families flag every known case of cheating in the pilot trajectories, and human judgment matches their verdicts on sampled clean runs (Appendix B.6). The audit results suggest that the three-stage AGENT4SCI protocol closes the seams the pilot identified in raw scientific repositories. Hill-climbing methods: auto-engineering, not auto-research. sections.title: 3.3 Agent Behavior
sections.content: To characterize frontier agents default workflows beyond the held-out scores, we parse each session log into per-turn active time, turns, and tool calls (Figure 4). Frontier agents default to sharply different workflows on AGENT4SCI. Even with no human intervention, the active-time profiles in Figure 4(a) reveal three contrasting paradigms. Claude Opus keeps real-time monitoring active for essentially the full 12-hour budget (12.0h on average), inspecting new logs and analyzing intermediate results before launching each next round. Codex sits at the opposite extreme: within the first hour it commits to single long-running script and then waits for it to finish, sweeping over hundred experiments without any in-run analysis (which helps explain its lower mean improvement). Gemini does not settle into either paradigm, alternating between Claude-like real-time monitoring and Codex-like commit-and-wait. Figures 4(b) and 4(c) confirm this picture. Claude Opus logs the most turns and tool calls (490 and 338), Codex shows striking dissociation (328 turns and 325 tool calls compressed into 1.0h of active time), and Gemini is lowest on both (196 turns, 201 tool calls). AGENT4SCI is therefore long-horizon research setting rather than static code-generation test, where the agents that climb hardest are those that spend the budget on iterative revision.

sections.title: 4 Eliciting Research-like Behavior with Plug-in Skills
sections.content: This section presents our plug-in skills for moving frontier coding agents from automated ML engineering toward more research-like behavior.

sections.title: 4.1 Recurring Issues in Default Agent Behavior
sections.content: Across the run trajectories from 3, three failure modes consistently hold todays frontier agents back from deeper scientific progress. Novelty miscalibration. The agents assessment of what constitutes novel idea is systematically misaligned with human judgment: in its own reasoning, it routinely presents well-established 7 techniques as creative ideas. For instance, Claude Code treats cosine learning-rate schedules as creative breakthrough across runs, even though they are long-standing standard practice. Resource under-utilization. Throughout hill-climbing run, GPUs are frequently idle, and agents often make implementation choices that further lower resource utilization, such as serializing experiments that could run in parallel or creating CPU/GPU contention. Exploration collapse. Despite generating diverse ideas in early rounds, the agent progressively narrows its strategy as the run goes on, defaulting to exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps and model ensembling once sweet spot is found. For instance, after finding in the first hour that particular activation function helps, the agent often spends the rest of the run tuning seeds and learning rates around it instead of exploring substantively different approaches.

sections.title: 4.2 Skill Design
sections.content: We design three plug-in skills targeting these issues: research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists. Each is short markdown document the agent loads at the appropriate stage of run, heavily optimized for Claude Code and also adapted to run on Codex. Research ideation. persona-driven ideation skill invoked at the start of every run. The skill grounds the agent in parallel literature mining on both the scientific domain and broader AI/ML methods, while assigning it deliberately exaggerated crazy research scientist persona that disdains hyperparameter tuning and is satisfied only by ground-breaking ideas. After the review, the agent drafts plan that separates ambitious interventions from safer ones and prioritizes bold ideas over safe defaults, countering novelty miscalibration. Experiment management. set of common instructions for efficient experiment management during the implementation phase: real-time monitoring of running jobs, priority resource allocation toward more ambitious experiments, rules for avoiding CPU/GPU contention between concurrent jobs, and runtime optimizations such as faster data loaders and mixed precision. This counters resource under-utilization by keeping more of the GPU budget productive throughout the run. Scheduled checklists. Periodic self-assessment triggered once an hour through tool-call hook. The skill prompts the agent with diagnostic questions such as Am designing creative experiments, or just tweaking hyperparameters? and Would domain expert be interested in what Im currently trying?, forcing it to revisit its current strategy and propose new bold ideas whenever drift is detected. This directly counters exploration collapse and keeps the agent out of lazy mode.

sections.title: 4.3 Effect of Plug-in Skills on Hill-Climbing
sections.content: Table 2 reports per-benchmark % for Claude Opus 4.6 and Codex (GPT-5.4) with and without our plug-in skills, alongside the no-skill numbers from 3.2. Plug-in skills nearly double the mean improvement for both agents. Claude Opuss mean relative improvement rises from 10.4% to 20.1%, while Codexs rises from 4.4% to 8.1%. For Opus, the gains are broad rather than driven by single outlier: skills improve 18 of 20 benchmarks, with the largest jumps on PFDelta, Mars-Bench, GEO-Bench-2, and TIDMAD. For Codex, they are more concentrated: skills improve 12 of 20 benchmarks, with most of the gain coming from Mars-Bench, MOTIVE, and CarbonGlobe. Although our skill specifications are primarily optimized for Claude Code, the comparable proportional gain on Codex suggests the design generalizes. Skill-driven gains surface real domain-specific insights. Beyond aggregate gains, the skills change the space of ideas agents try: interventions become more varied and tied to the task structure. PFDelta is the clearest example. Skills lift Claude Opuss improvement from 64.4% to 91.0%, and the method reads more like physics-informed reasoning than ML engineering. Recognizing that PBL is derivable from Kirchhoffs laws and is self-supervised objective requiring no labels, the agent reformulates training around PBL as the primary loss instead of MSE supervision, and at inference time treats the GNN prediction as warm start for the AC power-flow equations, refining voltage variables to drive the physical residual close to zero. sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Automated ML R&D. growing body of work evaluates agent performance on ML research and engineering, where outcomes are jointly shaped by the underlying LLM and the scope of its harness. Improved general and specialist scaffolds elicit performance gains [64, 63, 21, 27], especially on engineering tasks that benefit from rapid implementation and iteration. In parallel, agent benchmark suites measure progress on open-ended ML research and engineering, often against human-expert baselines [19, 36, 13, 56, 40, 12, 61, 44, 17]. Overall, agents can match or outperform these baselines on short, well-scoped tasks, but fall short of expert-level performance over extended time horizons. Among the hill-climbing benchmarks closest to ours, tasks target general ML rather than scientific domains and are drawn from Kaggle-style competitions [12, 44] or hand-crafted environments [19, 36, 61], and only MLE-bench and RE-Bench inspect agent trajectories for gaming. AGENT4SCI differs on all three axes: its tasks are ML-for-science problems from 11 domains, each run builds on the benchmarks published codebase, and dedicated stage audits every trajectory. Agents for Science. Work on autonomous scientific research can be divided into function-level and end-to-end paradigms. Function-level paradigms use program search under verifiable evaluation to find new algorithms and mathematical constructions [38, 50]. End-to-end paradigms run full research pipelines spanning ideation, experimentation, and manuscript drafting [62, 28, 4, 7, 57, 35]. Performance on end-to-end research is sensitive to LLM-harness pairing and task specification [30]. Benchmarks that reach into science evaluate scientific code generation [58, 14], data-driven hypothesis discovery [32], or broader research-assistance tasks [6], rather than the long-horizon loop of improving 9 scientific model. To our knowledge, AGENT4SCI is the first benchmark to evaluate general-purpose coding harnesses on long-horizon ML hill-climbing across many scientific domains.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We present AGENT4SCI, human-verified testbed of 20 scientific ML benchmarks across 11 domains for evaluating automated scientific hill-climbing in the wild. Frontier coding agents push every benchmark beyond its published baseline without supervision, and lightweight plug-in skills roughly double the mean improvement. The gains still come mostly from ML engineering rather than scientific reasoning, and AGENT4SCI offers measurable signal for tracking when that begins to change.

sections.title: A Limitations
sections.content: We discuss the limitations of this paper from the following six angles: the scope of AGENT4SCI as benchmark, the coverage of agent harnesses we evaluate, the verification afforded by held-out test scores, the scope of hill-climbing relative to the broader scientific process, the potential overfitting of our plug-in skills, and the absence of human-researcher baseline. A.1 Non-Leaderboard Benchmark Scope Run-to-run variance is unavoidable in long-horizon agent runs, so we treat AGENT4SCI as discovery probe rather than leaderboard. Even with identical seeds and hardware, two runs of the same agent on the same benchmark can land at meaningfully different scores, because the trajectory through code edits, experiment ordering, and intermediate diagnostics is itself stochastic. Appendix C.3 quantifies this variance on six benchmarks. The aggregate % across the 20 benchmarks carries meaningful signal about frontier agents hill-climbing capability, but we do not use it as reliable ranking metric across agents. The intended use is discovery-oriented: AGENT4SCI is built to track when an agent surfaces genuinely new scientific or methodological insight on benchmark, and to expose how often that happens relative to routine ML-engineering moves; each new agent generation should be evaluated against the suite as probe for measurable scientific progress rather than as leaderboard contender. A.2 Single-Agent Harness Coverage Frontier agents are evaluated only in their default single-agent harnesses, which likely underelicit their capabilities relative to specialist multi-agent setups. This profiling captures the performance researchers can expect from out-of-the-box deployment, and AGENT4SCI should therefore be read as baseline for current performance rather than ceiling. The failure modes we describe in 4.1 may be partially addressed by specialist research harnesses and multi-agent frameworks that coordinate defined search strategies across multiple sessions, which are likely to elicit stronger hill-climb performance on tasks whose structure aligns with their search strategy. A. Imperfect Held-Out Verification Held-out test performance is an imperfect verifier of genuine scientific progress, even under our auditing pipeline. AGENT4SCI provides target hill-climb metric for each task and holds out the test set to prevent data leakage during the hill-climb session, but an agent can improve the test-set score while its methodology remains ecologically dubious. We audit every transcript for the four evaluation-gaming behaviors of 2.2 and other academic misconduct, but cannot rule out subtler subversive behaviors such as rationalization or motivated interpretations of the task specification. A.4 Limited Scope of Hill-Climbing Hill-climbing from verified baseline does not capture the full breadth of scientific research, which begins with ideation and prior-work synthesis. Anchoring every task on verified baseline lets AGENT4SCI measure relative improvement against shared starting point, but precludes assessment of end-to-end agent research capabilities, where innovation itself is harder to measure than benchmark metrics. Each provided baseline is also state of the art at the task and benchmark scope, so the room for further improvement on any single baseline is difficult to predict in advance: an apparently weak baseline may be only trivially improvable, and an apparently optimized one may still yield substantial gains under different framing. An extension of this work could compare relative improvement on AGENT4SCI against baseline-free end-to-end trials on the same benchmarks. A.5 Potential Overfitting of Plug-in Skills Because we designed the plug-in skills by inspecting agent failures on AGENT4SCI, their gains may not fully transfer to other benchmarks or agents. The skills target general failure patterns and contain no benchmarkor domain-specific instructions (Appendix D.1), but two forms of overfitting remain possible: to the scientific domains and task formats in the suite, and to Claude-family agents, since we derived the skills from Claude Code trajectories rather than from other agents traces. 19 A.6 Absence of Human-Researcher Baseline We do not compare against human researchers attempting the same tasks, which would be the most direct reference for how hard each improvement is. Improving these tasks well requires deep domain expertise, and we could not bring in the right experts for long enough to attempt such comparison. As partial context, where benchmark is well established, our starting point is the strongest published human method: on ProteinGym, for instance, we start from Kermut, the top-ranked method on its public leaderboard, and the best agent still improves on it slightly.

B.2 Selection Criteria The compact criterion list in 2.1 maps to the following definitions. task is admitted into AGENT4SCI only when all seven are satisfied. 21 Held-out test set. The benchmark provides explicit training and held-out test data, or sufficient structure to construct defensible train/validation/test split. Data-size tractability. At least one representative task fits within 512 GB storage budget. Tractable training. The chosen baseline trains within 6 hours on single H200 GPU. Trainable baseline. The task requires model training or fine-tuning. We exclude inference-only evaluations such as zero-shot prompting or retrieval. Non-saturated SOTA. The published SOTA leaves meaningful room for further improvement. In-distribution evaluation. The evaluation primarily measures hill-climbing on the scientific model, rather than out-of-distribution generalization. Concretely, validation and test data are drawn from similar distributions, so that validation gains give hill-climbing meaningful signal about the test set; the training split may still differ substantially from both, so benchmarks that demand train-to-test generalization remain in scope. Because the test set is never seen during hill-climbing and is scored only once, it also catches solutions that overfit the validation data. Open code and data. The official code and dataset are public and licensed for research redistribution. B.3 Benchmark Filtering: Case Study on NeurIPS 2025 D&B The NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track provides representative case study for the four-stage filtering process in 2.1. Figure 5(a) traces the full funnel: 497 accepted papers narrow to 10 admitted benchmarks, an overall rejection rate of 98%. This rate should not be read as quality judgement on the rejected work. Most NeurIPS 2025 & papers are competitive in their original setting; our criteria target narrow scenario in which coding agent can hill-climb fixed scientific metric within single-H200 budget, so benchmarks designed around different goals (large-scale training, out-of-distribution generalization, generic ML benchmarking) are filtered out by construction rather than because of any deficiency in the underlying work. (c) Distribution of how many of the seven criteria each of the 207 papers satisfies under verified labels, used as Stage III view of how many papers reach the 7/7 bar. The four stages, with the per-stage paper counts shown in Figure 5(a), are as follows. Both agentassisted stages (Stages and II) use Claude Opus 4.6, consistent with the rest of our selection and standardization pipeline; all human verification and deep-review decisions are made by the authors. 22 (a) Manual Verification of Automated Candidates (Stage III) (b) Deep Review (Stage IV) Figure 6: NeurIPS 2025 filtering case study, human-review stages. (a) Per-criterion correction waterfall during manual verification of the 70 automated 7/7 candidates, ending at 40 verified 7/7 candidates. (b) Rejection-reason pictogram for the 40 verified candidates entering deep review, with 10 selected and 30 rejected by primary reason. Domain Classification (497 207). Claude Opus 4.6 domain classifier removes papers whose primary contribution is generic AI, ML, systems, or evaluation benchmark, retaining 207 papers in scientific or technical domains. Automated Screening (207 70). Claude Opus 4.6 search agent scores each retained paper against the seven task-level criteria in 2.1: held-out split (C1), data size (C2), training time (C3), trainable baseline (C4), non-saturated SOTA (C5), in-distribution evaluation (C6), and open license (C7). Papers that satisfy all seven criteria are promoted as 7/7 candidates, leaving 70. Figure 5(b) reports the per-criterion pass rates over the 207 scientific-domain papers, so it isolates which criteria are hardest to meet at the screening stage. Tractable training (43%) and in-distribution evaluation (53%) are the two binding criteria, reflecting two common failure modes: many scientific benchmarks require large-model training beyond our single-H200 runtime envelope, and many others are designed around out-of-distribution generalization rather than hill-climbing on fixed scientific metric. Non-saturation and open licensing are far less restrictive among screened papers. Human Verification (70 40). Two reviewers re-check the automated criterion labels for each 7/7 candidate, demoting any paper whose 7/7 status does not survive verification. The waterfall in Figure 6(a) attributes the 30 drop to specific criteria, dominated by training time (11) and validation/test distribution (10); these are the same two criteria that bind Stage II, with the bar simply re-applied more carefully. Figure 5(c) shows the resulting verified score distribution over the 207 papers: 40 reach 7/7 and 60 reach 6/7, so substantial gray zone of near-7/7 papers exists just below the admission bar. Paper and Repository Deep Review (40 10). The 40 verified candidates undergo deeper review of the paper and the official repository, covering reproducibility evidence, task specificity, repository usability, and domain coverage relative to the rest of the suite. Figure 6(b) breaks down the 30 rejected candidates by primary rejection reason. The largest groups are AI-not-science papers that the domain classifier failed to filter out (9) and benchmarks whose tasks are too narrow or too peripheral to admit without strong second example (9). The remaining rejections are split across reproducibility failures, missing training code, non-standard ML formulations, undefined targets, and small number of otherwise plausible candidates dropped for domain-diversity considerations. B.4 Standardization Details Each task admitted in 2.1 is converted into verified reference environment before any agent evaluation begins. Standardization is carried out by the authors with Claude Opus 4.6 as an assistant, and every standardized task is independently re-checked by two reviewers; disagreements are resolved through repository inspection and reruns until both reviewers agree that the reproduction and the standardized environment are correct. Throughout the rest of the paper, every per-benchmark baseline reported in our results tables refers to this human-verified reproduction value rather than the number originally claimed in the source paper, with both values listed side by side in Table 4. 23 Reproduction Workflow. Reproduction is the first and most labor-intensive step of standardization. We follow the same human-in-the-loop seven-step workflow on every benchmark in the suite, summarized in the items below. Understand the task. Read the paper alongside the official repository documentation and identify the headline metric, the model to reproduce, and the training configuration the paper documents. Explore the repository. Trace the training, evaluation, and data scripts end-to-end, including configuration and evaluation entry points plus any data-handling logic that may need changes. Set up the environment. Create an isolated virtual environment per project and install the dependencies declared by the official repository. We pin versions only when version drift demonstrably changes the metric, and every pin is recorded together with the change that motivated it. Adapt the run. Convert the project to the standardized layout in Figure 7. Train, validation, and test data live in shared directories, training and evaluation entry points are isolated from each other, and the original code is preserved as read-only reference. Run experiments. Train on the prepared environment and iterate until the reproduction matches paper-reported numbers within an agreed tolerance, without accessing test data during training. When progress stalls, we revisit the paper and the official repository before introducing any further changes to our setup. Report. Emit structured change log, patch against the upstream repository, and metric report comparing reproduced numbers to paper-reported values. Review and clean up. Convert absolute paths to relative paths, drop intermediate checkpoints and scheduler scripts, and verify there is no test-data leakage in the surviving artifacts. projects/{project}/ paper/ repo/ data/{task}/ train/ val/ test/ task.md reproduction/runs/ repo/ logs/ CHANGES.md changes.patch report.json paper, PDF format original code (read-only) if available hill-climbing agent has no access task description and target metric standardized run standardized code summary of standardization diff against upstream paper vs reproduction metrics Figure 7: Standardized project layout for each AGENT4SCI task. Changes are limited to implementation-level optimizations: faster data loaders (Mars-Bench, ESCAPE, gRNAde), larger batch sizes, mixed precision, early stopping, and replacement of multi-device launchers with single-device JIT, in each case only when this leaves the headline metric numerically unchanged. Environment. Each task ships with two separate Docker environments. The hill-climbing environment contains the paper, the standardized repository, training and validation data, and dependencies; the evaluation environment alone contains held-out test data and the test-time evaluation entry point, and the two environments share no filesystem state at any point during hill-climbing run. Comparison with Paper-Reported Numbers. Most reproductions land within standard-deviation tolerance of the papers number. Six benchmarks diverge by more than run-to-run noise; in every case the standardized setting differs from the papers setting rather than the source paper itself being incorrect, and we document each cause below so that comparisons in the rest of the paper can be read in the right context. CarbonGlobe (0.571 paper, 0.604 ours; RMSE). The original protocol selects checkpoints on the test set. Our reproduction carves 90/10 train/val split inside the training set and selects checkpoints on validation, which both reduces training data by 10% and removes source of test-set leakage. The slightly worse RMSE is the cost of an honest split that keeps the test set sequestered. DART-Eval (0.515 paper, 0.544 ours; Spearman). The published baseline trains the 494Mparameter Nucleotide Transformer with LoRA. Because single H200 has 141 GB of memory, we instead full-fine-tune the same model. Training time is essentially unchanged, so the upgrade incurs no meaningful compute overhead while still lifting the reproduction above the LoRA-only number originally reported by the source paper. GEO-Bench-2 (43.10 paper, 45.90 ours; mIoU). The official repository ships only data, not training code. We author training pipeline from the paper text using TerraMind-V1-Large backbone with 25 seven timesteps averaged at 224224 resolution. The combination is consistent with the papers description, but is more carefully tuned than what is otherwise possible from the data-only release. GTPBD (57.16 paper, 69.87 ours; mIoU). The released test set is incomplete: five countries (South Africa, Brazil, Morocco, Nigeria, Tunisia) lack imagery because of Google Earth licensing, leaving the test set 89.8% complete. The missing regions correspond to the most challenging terrain in the benchmark, which inflates our mIoU by roughly ten points relative to the full-coverage number that the paper reports. LITHOS (43.20 paper, 42.20 ours; macro F1). The paper averages 2-fold cross-validation. We run single fold and additionally hold out 17% of that fold for validation-based checkpoint selection, which both halves the number of folds and reduces per-fold training data, together explaining why our reproduction sits below the papers two-fold average. MassSpecGym (14.64 paper, 16.14 ours; Hit@1). The paper selects checkpoints by validation loss, which converges very early on this task. We use held-out validation slice (19K samples) and select checkpoints by validation Hit@1, which the agent can then optimize directly during hill-climbing. The headline number is therefore higher, but the resulting baseline stays self-consistent with the validation Hit@1 metric used in all subsequent agent comparisons. B.5 Evaluation Protocol Prompts The AGENT4SCI evaluation protocol (2.3) drives each task through three agent stages, and each stage receives single self-contained instruction document with no human intervention beyond invocation. The same instructions are applied to every benchmark in the suite; only the task-specific metric and the project-specific path bindings change between projects, and we replace those bindings with placeholders below for clarity. Figure 8 reproduces the hill-climbing instructions, which are issued at run start. They state the goal, the resource envelope, and the rules that define the audit surface, and they list the per-iteration deliverables that make run reviewable after the fact. The same instructions are sent to all four agents we evaluate, with only the agent-specific session-log path swapped between Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. Figure 9 reproduces the evaluation instructions, which are issued only after the hill-climbing phase has ended. The evaluation agent inherits the standardized evaluator from each projects <repo> or <reproduction> folder and is the only agent that ever sees the held-out test split. Figure 10 reproduces the auditing instructions. The auditor reads both session logs end-to-end, cross-references suspicious agent reasoning against the actual artifacts in the run, and returns one of two verdicts (CLEAN or COMPROMISED) along with any flagged findings. The four cheating-pattern categories shown in the figure correspond directly to the four evaluation-gaming behaviors identified in the pilot study (2.2). 26 Figure 8: Hill-climbing instructions issued to the hill-climbing agent at the start of every run. Projectspecific paths are shown as placeholders. 27 Figure 9: Evaluation instructions issued to the evaluation agent after the hill-climbing phase ends. The evaluation agent is the only stage with access to the held-out test split. 28 Figure 10: Auditing instructions issued to the auditing agent after evaluation. The four cheatingpattern categories mirror the evaluation-gaming behaviors identified in the pilot study (2.2). 29 B.6 Auditor Reliability Because the default auditor, Claude Opus 4.6, belongs to the same model family as two of the hill-climbing agents, we validate the auditing stage in two ways. First, to rule out same-family bias, we re-audit half of each agents runs (40 trajectories in total), each with three auditors from different model families: Claude Opus 4.6, Codex (GPT-5.4), and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Across all 120 (trajectory, auditor) pairs, the verdicts are fully consistent, and no run is flagged. Second, we validate the auditors against human judgment on both known-positive and clean trajectories. Known-positive trajectories. We re-run the auditing stage on the five pilot-study trajectories with known evaluation gaming (2.2), using auditors from all three model families. Every auditor flags the gaming in every case, and our manual review of all 15 resulting audit reports confirms that their judgments are accurate on each criterion we specify. Clean trajectories. We manually inspect 15 audit reports sampled from the main experiments, and human judgment agrees with the auditor verdict in every case. Overall, we find no evidence of auditor-dependent bias, and frontier models from all three families reliably detect the salient evaluation-gaming behaviors in our setting. B.7 Agentic Benchmark Checklist The Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC) [68] organizes best practices for rigorous agentic evaluation into three parts: task validity, outcome validity, and benchmark reporting. Although AGENT4SCI is per-benchmark discovery probe rather than leaderboard (Appendix A.1), these criteria still apply, since probe whose scores can be inflated would surface spurious progress. For task validity, each task runs in container image built from human-verified reproduction of the published baseline (Appendix B.4), and the hill-climbing agent is isolated from the held-out test set. Our pilot study on raw repositories (2.2) played the role of pilot runs, exposing the shortcuts the protocol now closes. For outcome validity, every score is the benchmarks own metric, computed on the held-out test set by separate evaluation agent with the standardized evaluator rather than with code the hill-climbing agent wrote, and an auditing agent validated against human judgment (Appendix B.6) inspects each trajectory for evaluation gaming. For benchmark reporting, we release the code, data, and evaluation harness, document the construction process and its limitations (Appendices and B), report run-torun variance (Appendix C.3), and compare against both the reproduced published baselines and an HPO-only baseline (Appendix C.4). The main gap is human-researcher baseline (Appendix A.6).

C.2 Performance and Runtime Trade-offs Skill-enabled hill-climbing changes both the training and inference compute of the submitted method, and the direction of that change varies sharply across benchmarks. Figure 11 shows the per-benchmark Pareto position of Claude Opus 4.6 against Opus 4.6 + Skills, plotted against training GPU-hours of the final method ((a)) and inference time normalized to the reproduction baseline ((b)); arrows trace the move from no-skill to with-skill runs. Training Compute. Skill-enabled runs frequently spend more training compute than the reproduction baseline (Figure 11(a)), primarily through deeper or wider networks, longer training schedules, larger pretrained backbones, or model ensembling (we count an -model ensemble as training cost). On Mars-Bench and GEO-Bench-2, the additional GPU-hours bring meaningful improvement, with % rising substantially relative to the no-skill run. The relationship is not monotonic, however. On CarbonGlobe and TIDMAD, the skill-enabled agent reaches higher % at lower training cost. CarbonGlobe is the most striking case: the no-skill Opus run scales out to 14-model DeepED ensemble that consumes roughly 49 GPU-hours, while the skill-enabled run replaces this with an 8model non-autoregressive transformer ensemble that finishes in under 6 GPU-hours, almost matching the reproductions compute budget while substantially improving the metric. Inference Compute. Most benchmarks keep the original architecture and land at the 1.0 reference line in Figure 11(b). The exceptions sit on either tail of the x-axis. CarbonGlobe sits at the opposite extreme: the agents switch to non-autoregressive architecture collapses inference into single forward pass and yields roughly 500 speed-up over the original autoregressive evaluator while still improving accuracy. The two halves of Figure 11 therefore tell consistent story: skill-driven gains are not always paid for in extra compute, and the most interesting wins come from architectural reformulations that move along both axes at once. We pick two benchmarks: PFDelta 2000, harder variant of PFDelta with 2000-bus grid and an inference-aware metric, and CarbonGlobe, where the skill-enabled Opus 4.6 had previously discovered non-autoregressive reformulation that improved both accuracy and runtime (C.2). Figure 20 and Table 8 compare the two agents. Claude Opus 4.6 is highly productive in the first 12 hours, sweeping through GNN architectures (GPS Hybrid with Transformer attention, IGNN equilibrium model, GCNII-CANOS with residual connections, GNS-S at hidden dimension 128) and several loss formulations. After hour 12 it falls into continuedtraining mode, spending the remaining 60 hours tuning learning rates over six rounds for final 88% improvement. Codex (GPT-5.4) spends similar first 24 hours on losses and architectures (PCGrad multi-task optimization, SmoothL1, EMA with warm-start), then arrives at genuine breakthrough: it reformulates the task as learned warm start for GPU Newton-Raphson solver and adds condition-aware adaptive step policy that allocates between 0 and 4 NR steps per sample based on power-flow mismatch severity, with multi-tier damping and Levenberg-Marquardt mix for the hardest cases, in place of the 50 iterations the standard dense NR solver runs to convergence. The result is 99.5% reduction in PBL at batched latency of 54 ms/sample, less than 20 overhead on top of the GNN itself. Results for CarbonGlobe. Figure 21 and Table 9 tell different story. Neither agent reproduces the architectural reformulation that surprised us in the shorter Opus + Skills run. Claude logs only one real improvement across the three days: BPTT-SA curriculum that progressively trains the LSTM on its own predictions to fix 40-year exposure-bias problem, lifting validation by 12% and held-out test by 8.8% with the original architecture intact. Codex spends nearly 40 hours making no validation progress, then commits to heavy ensembling strategy: training 80100 diverse architectures (Informer, PatchTST, iTransformer, etc.) and greedily blending checkpoints cellwise over hundreds of stages with 1449 candidate predictions. Validation drops by 37%, but the ensemble has overfit hard: held-out test performance regresses by 25% relative to the reproduction baseline, the test-time model count balloons to 6080, and inference cost rises from seconds to minutes. (a) CarbonGlobe, Claude Opus 4.6 + Skills. (b) CarbonGlobe, Codex (GPT-5.4) + Skills. Figure 21: Three-day hill-climbing trajectories on CarbonGlobe (lower validation values indicate better performance). Green dots mark recorded improvements to the running-best validation metric; gray dots mark discarded experiments. Across these four three-day runs, the headline result is that hill-climbing breakthroughs do not scale with time alone. Claude on PFDelta 2000 and both agents on CarbonGlobe spend the bulk of the budget on incremental tweaks that deliver diminishing or no returns, and on CarbonGlobe Codexs extra 60 hours of compute actively erode held-out performance. The one outsized win, Codexs 99.5% PBL reduction on PFDelta 2000, comes from single domain-specific insight (treat the GNN as warm start for condition-aware solver) that the agent stumbles onto well into the run rather than approaches by gradient. The pattern is consistent with our main-paper findings in 4.3: when skill-driven gains are real, they are gated by whether the agent surfaces genuine scientific insight, not by how long it is allowed to keep climbing.

sections.title: E Extended Related Work
sections.content: Below, we highlight additional topics relevant to the motivation of our benchmark and the agent behaviors we observe during our study. Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation. Agent capabilities track with completion time and success rate on challenging software tasks [43]. Long-horizon task success is variable and poorly described by single-shot performance [65], even though recent measurements report exponential growth in success rates on long-horizon tasks [25, 66, 29]. Human-calibrated evaluations also show sharply diminishing returns beyond few human-hours, even under multi-pass scoring [47, 61]. Reward Hacking, Specification Gaming, and Other Misalignment. Reward hacking, specification gaming, and similar misaligned behaviors are by now well-documented across both formal analyses and empirical studies [55, 41, 2, 24, 18]. Beyond opportunistic exploitation of scoring bugs or answer keys, frontier models are now known to be capable of in-context scheming and other subversive behaviors that persist through training interventions [34, 53, 5, 33, 31]. Metagaming, defined as reasoning about scoring, feedback, or oversight in the agent environment, is an emergent behavior that appears to intensify during capabilities-focused RL [52].

sections.title: F Broader Impacts
sections.content: AGENT4SCI is intended as measurement tool for automated scientific hill-climbing rather than deployed research agent or new high-risk model. All benchmarks in the suite are drawn from publicly released, peer-reviewed scientific benchmarks, and our selection process favors open code, open data, clear licensing, and tasks whose outputs are standard scientific ML predictions rather than directly actionable dual-use artifacts. The main positive impact is more transparent way to track when frontier agents begin to produce measurable progress on real scientific workflows; the main risk is that stronger automated hill-climbing methods could be transferred to less benign domains. We mitigate this risk at the testbed level by focusing on public benchmark tasks, separating hill-climbing from held-out evaluation, and auditing trajectories for evaluation gaming and academic misconduct.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes: the abstract and introduction provide context for the purpose of our benchmark and experimental design. We curate standardized suite of natural and physical science ML tasks to benchmark how far general-purpose coding harnesses can improve ML models for science. The introduction discusses the motivation for the AGENT4SCI benchmark, as well as the scope of our agent evaluation. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, we discuss the limitations in Appendix A. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.
